strengths: Addresses a core bottleneck in end-to-end embodied AI training by introducing Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation (EALM) to smoothly transition between imitation (DAgger) and reinforcement learning (PPO) without manual scheduling.

Proposes a well-designed auxiliary semantic segmentation task that encourages the transformer model to learn robust spatial and semantic features from RGB observations, significantly improving sample efficiency.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on the competitive HM3D-OVON benchmark among RGB-only mapless methods, showing remarkably close success rates on seen vs. unseen categories.

Provides a thorough practical analysis of adapting the policy to real-world deployment by using an open-vocabulary segmenter (YOLOE) and introducing clever filtering and threshold calibration strategies.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with highly detailed tables, training curves, hyperparameter lists, and statistical significance validation.
weaknesses: The policy shows heavy reliance on the quality of the external open-vocabulary detector. As shown in Table 4, there is a large performance gap when transitioning from ground-truth masks (70.4% SR) to YOLOE predictions (40.1% SR), highlighting the sensitivity to detection errors.

The evaluation lacks an analysis of total inference latency (FPS). Although the transformer policy is lightweight (130M parameters), running a heavy open-vocabulary segmentation model (YOLOE) at every frame can be computationally expensive for real-world robotic deployment.

The analysis of exploration behavior is somewhat limited. According to Table 11, the policy fails completely (0.1% SR) if the goal mask is omitted (zeroed out). This implies that the learned policy functions primarily as a local goal-seeking controller and may lack independent exploration strategies when the target object is not yet visible in the frame.

strengths: Introduces Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation (EALM), a novel and elegant way to dynamically balance imitation (DAgger) and reinforcement (PPO) learning based on policy entropy, avoiding heuristic manual phase switching.
Delivers solid empirical results on the HM3D-OVON benchmark, establishing state-of-the-art results for RGB-only mapless approaches on unseen categories.
Provides thorough ablation studies examining training strategies, observation components, and adaptation to predicted segmentation models.
The paper is highly detailed, well-structured, and includes comprehensive reproducibility details, including hyperparameters, statistical significance tests, and training curves in the appendix.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on the external open-vocabulary segmenter: The ablation in Table 11 shows that when the goal mask is omitted (Text Goal only), the navigation performance completely collapses to a 0.1% Success Rate. This indicates that the policy itself has virtually zero open-vocabulary visual-grounding capability; the open-vocabulary aspect is entirely outsourced to the external detector (YOLOE). The policy functions essentially as a local 'mask-follower' rather than a VL-grounded agent. This characteristic should be more explicitly highlighted in the main text.

Heuristic adaptation/calibration for segmentation: To achieve good performance with predicted segmentation, the authors rely on filtering masks by size and manually calibrating confidence thresholds per category (e.g., 0.4 for 'dishwasher' vs 0.01 for 'book'). This calibration process seems highly dataset-dependent and might limit the system's truly open-vocabulary generalization in the wild where confidence thresholds for novel categories are unknown.

Conceptual justification of the auxiliary segmentation head: Since the target binary mask $M_t$ is already provided as an input to the policy network, the auxiliary task of reconstructively predicting $M_t$ (using a DCGAN head) is essentially a reconstruction of an input. The authors should clarify why this specific self-reconstruction task provides a useful gradient signal rather than just forcing the model to copy the input mask.

strengths: The proposed Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation (EALM) is an elegant and automated mechanism to balance imitation learning and reinforcement learning based on policy entropy, successfully avoiding brittle heuristic phase-switching.

The method achieves strong empirical results on the HM3D-OVON benchmark, establishing state-of-the-art performance in the mapless, RGB-only category without relying on depth, odometry, or large Vision-Language Models.
The paper is highly thorough in its evaluations, including comprehensive ablation studies, detailed training curves, statistical significance tests, and category-level threshold analyses.
Integrating semantic segmentation both as an input target mask and as an auxiliary training loss is shown to greatly improve training sample efficiency and collision safety.
weaknesses: High dependency on the external segmenter: Table 11 shows that when the mask input is zeroed out, the success rate collapses to 0.1%. This suggests the policy is primarily acting as a 'mask follower' and has outsourced almost all semantic grounding to the external open-vocabulary detector (YOLOE). The policy itself does not appear to possess robust text-to-visual grounding.

Potential test/validation category calibration leak: The authors calibrate confidence thresholds of YOLOE for categories in the navigation vocabulary to boost performance (Table 4). Doing this for categories in the validation sets (especially unseen categories) violates the strict open-vocabulary zero-shot paradigm, as it assumes prior access to the target categories for threshold tuning.

Limited architectural novelty: Using target binary masks or pixel-level goal coordinates as conditioning inputs is relatively common in modern modular/hybrid navigation methods (e.g., PixelNav), making the technical contribution of the network architecture somewhat incremental.

Lack of exploration analysis: Since the policy relies heavily on the mask, it is unclear if the text goal actually guides the exploration phase when the target is not yet visible (and the mask is empty), or if the agent simply performs random exploration until YOLOE triggers a detection. An analysis of search efficiency prior to first detection would help clarify this.

strengths: Demonstrates state-of-the-art open-vocabulary object goal navigation performance on the HM3D-OVON benchmark (44.7% SR, 20.6% SPL on unseen categories) using only RGB inputs, without requiring depth, odometry, or heavy vision-language models.

Proposes Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation (EALM), which automatically and smoothly balances imitation learning (DAgger) and reinforcement learning (PPO) using policy entropy, avoiding heuristic and unstable manual phase switching.

Provides a comprehensive strategy to adapt the policy trained on ground-truth masks to noisy predicted masks from an off-the-shelf open-vocabulary segmenter (YOLOE) through auxiliary loss, semantic area rewards, and category-wise threshold calibration.
Includes thorough validation, containing statistical significance tests, detailed ablation studies, and physical real-world robot deployment on an iRobot Create 3 platform.
weaknesses: The navigation agent relies heavily on the quality of the external open-vocabulary segmentation model. Performance drops significantly when transitioning from ground-truth masks to predicted ones (from 69.3% to 44.7% SR), showing that perception remains a key bottleneck.

The use of the proposed semantic reward and fine-tuning on predicted masks increases the average collision count (e.g., from 29.4 to 45.4 collisions in Table 3). This trade-off between success rate and safety (collisions) is a practical concern, also reflected in the real-world trials where risky behavior near the goal was observed.

Clarification is needed for Equation (4): it is unclear if the ground-truth mask area $b_t$ is required during real-world deployment, or if it is strictly utilized as a simulator-only training reward.

strengths: State-of-the-Art Performance: The proposed OVSegDT establishes state-of-the-art results on the competitive HM3D-OVON benchmark (44.7% SR and 20.6% SPL on unseen categories) utilizing only RGB input, outperforming several methods that rely on additional sensors (depth, odometry) or larger Vision-Language Models.

Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation (EALM): The introduction of EALM provides a principled, automatic, and smooth transition between imitation learning (DAgger) and reinforcement learning (PPO) based on policy uncertainty (entropy). This is a well-designed training paradigm that eliminates brittle manual scheduling and improves both convergence and safety (reducing collisions during training).

Effective Sim-to-Real Adaptation: The paper presents practical strategies to bridge the performance gap between ground-truth and predicted segmentation masks, combining a semantic area-based reward, auxiliary segmentation loss, and confidence threshold calibration. This is thoroughly validated with hardware deployment on an iRobot Create 3 with a Jetson Orin.

Rigorous Ablation Studies: The ablation studies and failure analyses are extensive. They compare multiple imitation/reinforcement switching strategies, input modalities, loss components, and adaptation policies, which solidifies the claims made in the paper.
weaknesses: Scalability of Open-Vocabulary Calibration: The method relies heavily on calibrating the confidence thresholds of the external segmentation model (YOLOE) for different object categories in the navigation vocabulary. In a truly open-vocabulary, dynamic real-world deployment, pre-calibrating thresholds for arbitrary user-defined query phrases is impractical. It remains unclear how the model behaves on completely uncalibrated, dynamically queried unseen categories and what default threshold would be robust.

High Collision Rates: As highlighted in Table 3 and Table 4, incorporating the target mask and semantic reward leads to a significant increase in the average number of collisions per episode (nearly doubling from 29.4 to 45.4). While success rates are high, such safety degradation is a concern for actual physical deployment.

High Sensitivity to External Perception: The framework exhibits a massive performance drop (from 69.3% SR with GT masks to 28.8% SR with out-of-the-box YOLOE) before the proposed fine-tuning and calibration are applied. This highlights that the navigation policy is heavily bottlenecked by the external segmentation module, making it highly dependent on the quality of the selected open-vocabulary detector.

strengths: The proposed method, OVSegDT, establishes a new state-of-the-art on the competitive HM3D-OVON benchmark for RGB-only models, achieving 44.7% SR and 20.6% SPL on the unseen validation set.

The proposed Entropy-Adaptive Loss Modulation (EALM) is a well-designed, automated method to transition between imitation learning (DAgger) and reinforcement learning (PPO) based on policy uncertainty, avoiding brittle manual scheduling.

Comprehensive experimental analysis, including extensive ablation studies on training objectives, adaptation strategies for predicted segmentation, error category profiling, and statistical significance testing.
Real-robot validation demonstrating that the model trained in simulation can transfer to physical platforms (iRobot Create 3) with real-time inference capabilities on embedded hardware (Jetson Orin).
weaknesses: High dependency on upstream segmentation accuracy: As shown in the ablations (Table 4), when transitioning from ground-truth masks to predicted ones (using YOLOE out-of-the-box), the success rate drops drastically from 69.3% to 28.8% before fine-tuning/calibration.

The adaptation process requires category-specific confidence calibration for the object detector/segmenter, which might limit the seamless open-vocabulary generalization in practical applications when encountering completely novel, uncalibrated categories.

High collision count: Even with the proposed RL training and auxiliary losses, the final agent still registers high collision rates (averaging over 45 collisions per episode on unseen categories, Table 3), which remains a significant safety concern for real-world deployment.
